issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, this appraisal is a poor thematic fit because it implies an interpersonal perpetrator threat ('who will harm you') rather than danger from impersonal environmental forces. The rest of the profile is built around disaster-related ongoing danger/hypervigilance and intrusive reliving, so this item stands out as clinically incongruent with the specified trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a natural disaster trauma, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The memory and threat items describe classic fear-based re-experiencing and hypervigilance, but there is no accompanying content suggesting perpetration, moral injury, or a specific action during the disaster that would plausibly drive a strong violated-values appraisal.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'I have failed in my most important role in life' could occur after a disaster, but here it sits awkwardly with the otherwise generic fear/reliving profile. There are no memory or threat items about failing to protect family, losing dependents, or role-related guilt, so this item lacks support from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: 'I need to stay alert' while trying to sleep is more characteristic of an ongoing human threat context than of a completed natural disaster, especially when paired with scanning exits and staying near exits in all buildings. Taken together, these threat items imply anticipation of intentional attack or entrapment rather than the specific threat structure suggested by the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: 'Failed Role' is not impossible, but it is the least coherent appraisal in this profile for a 65-year-old married male retail worker with natural-disaster trauma. The rest of the profile centers on ongoing danger, hypervigilance, and intrusive reliving; this item instead implies a specific role-based self-evaluation that is not supported by the other selected appraisals, memory, threat, or coping items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: 'Other-Blame Rumination' sits awkwardly with a natural-disaster trauma profile. Blame can occur, but this item specifically focuses on dwelling on what other people have done to me, whereas the rest of the profile describes threat and reliving linked to impersonal environmental danger rather than interpersonal harm or betrayal. Without any corroborating appraisal or memory content involving preventable human actions, this item is clinically hard to reconcile.

vignette:
Kwame's Vigilance

Kwame was sixty-five years old when Hurricane Helene made landfall near his home in coastal North Carolina. He had worked retail for forty-two years-first as a stock clerk, then as a floor supervisor at a large electronics store in Wilmington-and he prided himself on his reliability. On the morning of the hurricane, he had driven his wife Ama to her sister's house inland, then returned alone to secure the store. The wind was already fierce, the sky a sickly green-grey. He was checking the loading dock doors when the wall of the building adjacent to theirs collapsed. The sound was immense, a roar and a crack, and Kwame felt the shock wave push him backward. He watched through the store windows as debris-wood, metal, a section of corrugated roof-spiraled through the air. For several seconds he stood frozen, watching the chaos unfold with the terrible clarity of someone who knows he might die in the next moment. Then he ran.

He made it to his car and drove to Ama's sister's house with his hands shaking. The store was damaged but repairable. Kwame was not. In the weeks that followed, he returned to work-the store reopened after three weeks-but something had fundamentally shifted in how he moved through the world. What had struck him most viscerally during those seconds at the loading dock was his complete powerlessness. The building could fail. The sky could fall. There was no warning that mattered, no way to predict or prevent catastrophe. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous, that safety was an illusion he had been foolish enough to trust. This conviction-that he could be destroyed at any moment by forces beyond his control-shaped everything that followed.

Because Kwame was certain the world remained perilously unsafe, he began to take precautions. He arrived at the store each morning and immediately scanned the ceiling, the walls, the structural supports. He positioned himself near the exit whenever possible, a habit so ingrained that he no longer consciously chose it; his body simply gravitated toward the door. When he walked through the stockroom, he noted the fire exits. When he sat in the break room, he mentally mapped the quickest route out. He found himself constantly scanning the environment for signs of threat-a crack in the plaster, a wobble in a shelf, the way the fluorescent lights hummed. These vigilant routines felt necessary, even protective. They were his answer to the conviction that disaster could strike without warning. If he stayed alert, if he stayed near the exit, perhaps he could escape the next time.

But Kwame's hypervigilance came at a cost. His sleep deteriorated almost immediately. He would lie awake beside Ama, his body tense, his mind unable to settle. He had come to believe that he needed to stay alert even at night, that lowering his guard was dangerous. His difficulty falling asleep was not simple insomnia; it was the biological expression of his certainty that danger lurked. The more he stayed awake, scanning the darkness of their bedroom for threats, the more convinced he became that his vigilance was justified-that something terrible would happen if he allowed himself to truly rest.

His memories of those seconds at the loading dock had taken on a peculiar quality. When they surfaced-and they surfaced constantly, unbidden, during quiet moments at work or in the car-they felt not like memories but like present reality. The sound of the collapse would replay in his mind like a film stuck on a loop, and in those moments, Kwame was not remembering the hurricane; he was back there, feeling the shock wave, watching debris spiral. The memory felt as immediate and dangerous as the original event. And because the memory felt present, not past, his body responded as if the threat were current. His heart would race. His breathing would shallow. This physiological arousal, in turn, seemed to confirm that danger was real and imminent, which intensified his conviction that he had to remain vigilant, that the world was as dangerous as he feared. Each time the memory replayed and his body reacted, it reinforced his belief that permanent damage had been done to him-that he could no longer trust his own safety, his own sense of security.

The scanning, the positioning near exits, the constant environmental checking-these strategies gave Kwame a fragile sense of control. But they also kept him trapped. The more he scanned, the more threats he seemed to find. The more he stayed near the exit, the more his nervous system remained primed for escape. His coworkers had begun to notice his restlessness, his refusal to work in the back stockroom for more than a few minutes at a time. His supervisor had asked if he was feeling alright. Kwame could not explain that he was no longer the man they had known, that something fundamental in him had fractured and could not be repaired. He was sixty-five years old, and he was afraid of his own workplace. He was afraid of buildings. He was afraid of the sky. He was afraid that one day, without warning, the world would collapse again-and this time, no exit would save him.
